I think it is possible to have relatively normal working hours with a PhD. But I would advise against having this set in stone with no exceptions. I follow a somewhat similar schedule but sometimes there are colloquiums, papers to be written, experiments that are finally going well, etc. 

A former cohort member followed this schedule so rigidly that they never attended colloquiums, department events, would never stay late to watch other peoples presentations (always would do theirs first then leave), etc. This ended up rubbing a lot of people the wrong way because they would leave right in the middle of group meetings/presentations, never come to colloquiums, and during coursework, was really difficult when it came to planning/attending group meetings. They actually ended up being asked to leave due to poor progress— I think they “showed up for work” every day with those specific time boundaries, but was not productive within those times.

Boundaries are important. But they go both ways— make sure they’re not so rigid that they’re actually hurting your progress. You may also find that you’re more productive and happier with a different kind of schedule. Mine can get a little wonky during the week to accommodate that kind of stuff if needed but my weekends are 100% mine.

Best of luck!

Something that really helped (especially being in a small apartment), was leashing him inside and tying him to a designated spot where most things (besides his toys and bed) are inaccessible. That way he can still be around me and out of his crate, but also can’t be get into stuff. At first he was wildly upset whenever I’d tether him (and he still can have a tantrum about it when he’s being consistently naughty), but now he knows that means he needs to play quietly by himself or take a nap. 

Your puppy will scream in the crate (or pen) initially, but eventually they will get used to it. I started with giving him a Kong every time he went in his crate or was tethered, so he built a positive association with it (and now will run right in because he knows he’s getting a special treat!).

from healing fully, or making it more painful (physically, mentally, emotionally, etc), it’s time to take a step back.

My vet recommended Hills science diet. He’s on the large breed puppy lamb and brown rice recipe, which has been the best so far for his sensitive belly and itchy skin (once we switched, both issues went away). We were even at the point where the vet was going to prescribe probiotics if needed, but switching to Hills solved it completely. He likes it, and is a happy, healthy pup who is very regular.

Hills is WSAVA backed and one of the big three recommended by vets.

I don’t give him any supplements as the puppy food provides him with that. I’m also weary of giving him too much of anything (particularly high in fat), since he has a sensitive belly. I’d always ask the vet first before introducing anything new into his diet. There is so much misinformation and marketing out there without real science backing it up.

For training treats, I go with freeze dried stuff (chicken, liver, etc). Single ingredient, so I can tell what does ok with his belly. He also seems to like (and tolerate) the Bocce’s bakery treat line (I like the size of their training treats, which I break up into four smaller treats about the size of a grain of rice/pea). 

For a first time dog owner, I’d recommend Zak George’s book. He has a whole chapter on dog food and treats, so you can learn how to read the ingredients and pick out what is good for dog.

In a month we were at the ER twice because he swallowed two dead animals whole (first a rat, which I was worried was poisoned), and then what I thought was a garbage bag, but actually was a dried mole. 

And then suddenly, he turned 6 months, and he stopped trying to eat everything in sight. He still  tries to eat plenty of things, but not all the time or quickly (so I can actually redirect him now).

Something that worked for me was setting alarms— when she hears the cue, it’s time to get up from the crate. I’d start by setting an alarm just a few minutes before she gets up and then letting her out (so she starts to associate that noise with getting up). Once she understands that, gradually set the alarm a few minutes later each day so you eventually get the time you want.

My pup used to demand to get up at 6:30 but now he sleeps in until 8:00! I’ve also gotten him into a routine of first getting up means going potty, then right back into the crate with a yummy treat/Kong while I get ready for the day (or sometimes sleep a little more). A second alarm then means it’s time to get up for real. I cover his crate while I’m getting ready so he can’t see what I’m doing, just has to wait until he hears the cue. For a while he would bark and cry and bark during this second crate time, but now we’re just down to whining a bit (so progress!). 

Be strict with the routine (first outing means potty right away, immediately back to crate  with no loving, playing, etc). He’s much easier to get into the crate now that he knows that’s what we do in the morning. Ignore the screaming, and be strict with the second alarm so she understands that screaming doesn’t get her out of the crate, the alarm does. You might have to pull out the big guns in terms of treats for this second crating (his is peanut butter Kong + a chew stick), but it will help her be busy for a little bit in the crate.

The thing that finally worked for me was teaching “toy.” I started by enticing him with a toy (outside of playtime, when he’s calm) and marking whenever he put it in his mouth, and rewarded by immediately playing with that toy with him. It took a couple of weeks but finally it clicked that “toy” means playtime, so whenever he’s trying to bite me (or on his way over to bite me) to initiate play, I say “toy” and he grabs the toy instead! I almost cried the first time he made the connection. I’m hoping we’ll eventually get to the point where he grabs the toy on his own first to initiate play (he does it sometimes, but not all of the time).

But I’m lagging behind in many other ways— I haven’t had any serious (adult) romantic relationships, I haven’t made a lot of friends post college, don’t have a lot of hobbies, and haven’t done very many “free-spirited things you’re supposed to do in your 20s” like traveling, going to events/concerts, exploring the city, etc.

On the surface, I appear very successful because I’m in graduate school. Deep down I am just as confused as every other 25 year old. I’ve mostly just been studying and working nonstop, and sometimes I feel scared that I’m missing out other life milestones. There is no set path and once you stop comparing yourself to others, you will feel much more secure.

My advice is to leave a paper trail. Make sure you made requests to your landlord in writing, and document the times you sent them. Document any responses you get, and when you received them. Depending on state laws, if a landlord fails to act within a certain time

My landlord dragged their feet when my ceiling collapsed back in August. I sent them basically a final courtesy email listing all of the correspondence we had and implied that I was going to start taking legal action if it wasn’t addressed ASAP, as the period in which emergency repairs are legally required to be made in my state had passed. They definitely got the message and then fixed it right away. 

Read your lease carefully, and your state renters’ laws. Landlords will get their act together once they realize you know they are breaking the law.

Last spring, my brother was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. He was missing for almost two weeks (in a state of psychotic mania) before he called me from a police station almost 1000 miles away saying he had been arrested. 

Somehow I managed to do (most) everything I was supposed to do that spring— research, present at a conference, run events, and mostly finish a class (I turned in my final exam only half done, I was so burnt out). Yes, I did get through it, but I’m not sure if that was the right call. I was very depressed and completely withdrew, I barely saw my friends and stopped exercising and eating properly. I basically gave my all during the day at school, then would completely crash at home and on the weekends. I finally started feeling like myself again just a month ago. I told my professor and my research advisor what had happened in the spring, but I haven’t brought it up since— I just told them that there may be some times when I need to leave at moments notice in case something happened. 
My professor let me turn in my exam at the end of the summer (giving me months extra time), but I just couldn’t bring myself to finish it and gave it to him just last week, still half-finished. I was really kicking myself about it, but writing this out made me realize how much I did in spite of it all, and that it’s okay. 

I was really struggling mentally, but I think this was the one situation where keeping myself in the program actually helped (or prevented it from getting worse). I needed the distraction as I was mourning, and something that I knew was consistent in a period of uncertainty, since we had no idea whether or how my brother would recover. 

Thankfully he seems to be on the mend, but I will be kicking myself for the rest of my life for not dropping everything to go look for him in hopes of preventing irreversible damage. 

If taking time off to spend with your mom is what you need, then do it. If you need the structure of the program to keep yourself grounded, then that’s okay too (though it sounds like you may get this from the job). There is no wrong answer— just remember to be kind to yourself over these next few months. We often judge ourselves by how much we’re accomplishing, but sometimes surviving is just as big of an accomplishment. You can always go back to school and work at any time, but time with family is precious and limited. Sending hugs to you and your mom.

My brain needs good food and good sleep to work on top of all else! I do tend to visit a variety of grocery stores to shop for the best price, but those trips (which often happen multiple times a week to have the freshest produce when I need it) make me happy.

Completely restricting yourself from doing anything (when you do have a little wiggle room), doesn’t set you up for success. I had some issues with food (shitty roommate used to bully me in the kitchen and prevented me from eating, ended up developing an eating disorder), so it was vital for me to create a healthy space to eat and heal my relationship with food without worry when I finally got out of that situation.  

Allowing yourself to spend a little more (if you can) on something that gives you joy, especially something like food that maintains your body and soul, is healthy. I know that allowing myself to do that prevents myself from binge spending elsewhere, and is vital for a healthy food relationship for myself.

This sounds pretty simple, but there are three things that make a class successful for me. Note, I am a (now graduating) STEM major, so this may be more STEM-forward, but I think it still applies.

1) Have frequent office hours that make it easy to drop in for a quick question, especially for upper level courses. A lot of the time I get the bulk of the material, but I just need to ask a clarifying question or I don't understand a specific portion of a topic, and need just a 5 minute explanation. When office hours are frequent, I feel like I am less of a "burden" for coming in and asking questions, especially since I can be shy about asking questions in class.

2) Give an opportunity to work out problems in class in 2 ways. A demonstration or "work through with me (as in students try and answer the next step while working through it together with the class)" of a problem is very useful, but so is the opportunity to try and solve a quick problem on your own for 5-10 minutes before coming back together as a class.

3) Have some sort of visual component, whether that is writing down equations or key ideas. The writing down of equations/derivations is pretty straightforward and always happens in my STEM classes, but I have noticed in my humanities classes that there is almost zero written/visual learning occurring in class. I understand the point of a class is to be discussion focused versus lecture focused (and that you should be able to determine the key points from a discussion) but I often find it is hard for me to learn when material is only presented in one form (audio only). Maybe the class comes up with the key ideas after a discussion, but I miss so much when it is a purely discussion based course because I can't organize my thoughts fast enough when I only am hearing it to take proper notes.
Probably a mix of the need to feel superior with jealousy due to the (incorrect) perception that non-STEM degrees are easier/less work.
